claims.statement: Sesam represents entities as dictionaries with string keys and literal, list, or dictionary values; an entity's required _id is a string primary key, not a typed NI or URI.

A dataset is an append-only immutable entity-version log supported by primary and secondary indexes; a normal dataset write appends only new or content-changed entities and drops candidates identical to the latest version using content-hash comparison.
A scheduled pipe pump pulls entities from a source, passes them through transforms, and sends the results to a sink.

Sesam is primarily an asynchronous batching and stream-processing system; its Service API is not designed or guaranteed for highly concurrent, low-latency, high-throughput user-facing applications, for which the documentation recommends a dedicated publishing system.
The normal dataset sink defaults its dataset id to the pipe id, creates an absent dataset when entities are written, and prohibits dataset ids containing / or targeting system: datasets.

A dataset source requires a dataset id and defaults include_previous_versions to false, returning only the latest version per unique _id; previous-version reads cannot recover history reclaimed by compaction.

Dataset sources have fixed supports_since, is_since_comparable, and is_chronological values of true; the public _updated contract allows string or integer tokens, requires consumers to treat them as opaque, and permits passing them back as HTTP since.
Normal dataset writes assign dataset-local incremental _updated values to versions, and a successfully completed pump saves the newest processed _updated as its since position.

A sink dataset becomes populated when its initial offset is set; the default if-source-populated policy waits for a populated source and consumption of all source entities, while dataset source require_populated_input defaults false and gates execution on population when true.
Dataset sink enable_optimistic_locking compares incoming _updated tokens with previous versions; if any token does not match, an error is raised and no entities are written to the target dataset.
The replicated_dataset sink preserves upstream entity sequence order and offsets unlike the normal writer, but does not support deletion tracking, entity re-posting, or circuit breakers.
JSON Pull returns entities as a JSON array even for a single entity; since starts after a supplied stream offset and limit caps the number of returned entities.
X-Dataset-Filtered marks a filtered JSON Pull stream in which the entity at X-Dataset-Max-Updated is not guaranteed to appear; the latter header is the highest committed dataset offset, JSON encoded.

Dataset recreation assigns a new generation UUID exposed through X-Dataset-Generation; backup restoration assigns a restore UUID and exposes the highest committed offset at restoration through restore headers.

Secondary indexes are maintained automatically and declared by hops join expressions, subset definitions, or explicit dataset sink configuration; orphaned indexes currently require UI or API deletion.

Dataset subsets behave as datasets in sources and hops and are implemented by secondary functional indexes, with one subset per indexed key; almost all deterministic DTL expressions that do not reference other datasets are supported.

A dataset source subset must be an eq expression with an index expression on the left and a literal value on the right; version 2 indexes are required for subset delete support because version 1 indexes do not support deletes.
Subset equality follows join equality, where any overlapping scalar or list value succeeds; null values and deleted entities are not indexed for joins and are not traversed by them.

Dataset sink indexes set to "$ids" maintains alternative-identity lookup for the dataset browser through _id and $ids; service global_defaults.always_index_ids enables this by default and itself defaults false.

Compaction defaults to retaining two unique versions per entity; keeping fewer than two makes dependency tracking best-effort and may miss reprocessable entities, with rescans recommended as a countermeasure, while keep_versions zero requires a time threshold.
Compaction is bounded by the lowest dependency-tracking offset on a dataset, and disabled pipes doing dependency tracking also hold back compaction.
Dependency tracking is supported only for pipes using a dataset source because tracked entities must be looked up by id before a specific point in time and re-fed through the pipe.

Retention and durability address different risks: compaction chooses which log versions remain, whereas durable data uses high-durability storage to reduce infrastructure-related loss of pipe data and state.
Underscore-prefixed fields are reserved only at entity root level; normal dataset writes ignore them except _id and _deleted, while child entities may contain underscore fields.

The dataset-generated _hash is a string used for change detection; only _id and _deleted among reserved root fields contribute to it, while ordinary fields including semi-reserved $ fields are stored and hashed.
Only _deleted true marks an entity deleted; a dataset deletion writes a tombstone version rather than physically removing all entity versions.
The dataset generates _previous as the previous version's _updated token; missing or null means no previous version, and a non-null pointer may reference history already removed by compaction.

The dataset generates _ts as an integer number of microseconds since 1970-01-01 UTC describing when the entity was added; it is informal metadata, not the opaque continuation token or an application modification date.
_tracked true is a legacy dependency-tracking materialization marker; the newer implementation does not require modifying entities, so the field is not a current tracking-status contract.
$ids contains alternative identities as NI values and the merge source collects merged identities in it, without replacing the required string _id.

create-child adds child entities to $children and emit_children expands them to standalone entities; dataset sink track_children compares against the previous version and produces deltas for incremental child deletion detection, inferred true when create-child is used unless overridden false.
The Entity Data Model's reserved-field prototype and standard Entity example contain malformed authored syntax and should not be treated as executable JSON.

Dataset sink deletion_tracking defaults true and, after a full run or rescan, writes deleted versions for entities that existed before the run but were not seen during it; this disappearance test is not absence from one incremental batch.

A failed DTL filter stops further DTL transforms; with a dataset sink it emits _filtered true to delete an existing not-already-deleted entity even during incremental synchronization, while unsupported sinks discard the entity instead of receiving it.

DTL filter does not stop entities already emitted by create, subsequent pipe transforms must handle _filtered carefully, and explicit _deleted is recommended when controlling deletion content directly.
The dataset sink suppress_filtered early-suppression optimization should only be used when a pipe produces exactly one output version per _id.

When a merge's resulting identity changes, the merge source emits deletes for obsolete ids with $replaced true; this is identity replacement rather than a real business deletion, and dataset source include_replaced false suppresses it while the default true retains it.
compaction.ttl_deletes_hours makes a deleted entity eligible for reclamation after the configured number of hours; reclamation removes all versions of that entity.

compaction.retract defaults false; when enabled with output $retract true it irreversibly removes all earlier versions in the sink dataset, retains the current version and deletion state, is idempotent, and overrides keep_versions per entity.

Retraction affects only the pipe's sink dataset, not upstream datasets or external consumers; $retract may be dropped by merge sources or emit_children, so downstream pipes honoring retraction need it explicitly in output and compaction.retract enabled.
Dataset source if_source_empty defaults accept, allowing deletion of previously synchronized entities on empty input; fail instead fails the run and avoids those deletions.
Merge source equality rules infer sameness transitively across datasets; null or empty-list equality results do not cause merging.
Equality rules added after a merge source has processed entities do not retroactively merge those entities; reset or rescan is required to apply the new rules to them.
Sesam Integers have unlimited range, Decimals arbitrary precision, and Floats IEEE 754 binary64 double precision that can lose precision; lists can contain heterogeneous nested values.

The documented maximum String length is 4294967296 bytes, distinct from the default stored entity-size limit of 104857600 bytes configured through dataset sink max_entity_bytes_size or the service global default.
Sesam serializes NaN and positive or negative infinity values in entities as null rather than invalid JSON.

Supported Transit extension literals serialize as JSON strings with ~ plus a tag: NI ~:, URI ~r, Date/Datetime ~t, Bytes ~b, UUID ~u, and arbitrary-precision Decimal ~f; Bytes payloads are base64 and UUIDs hexadecimal text.

The Transit Date range is ~t0001-01-01 through ~t9999-12-31; Datetime supports up to nanosecond precision, requires date and time plus UTC Z, permits an optional fractional second, and has documented bounds ~t0001-01-01T00:00:00Z through ~t9999-12-31T23:59:59.123456789Z.
Only the documented Transit extension types are supported; unknown Transit types are treated as strings, and Sesam currently does not support escaping string literals starting with ~.

Mixed-type ordering ranks Null, Boolean, Integer/Float/Decimal, Date/Datetime, UUID, NI, URI, String, Dict, Tuple, and Bytes in that order; compatible types sharing a rank sort together by value, incompatible types by rank, and Dict ordering sorts keys then compares key/value pairs.

The entity type documentation is internally inconsistent about orderability: its Standard types table calls Dict, List, and Null not orderable, but its focused Mixed type ordering section ranks Null and Dict and defines Dict comparison; that section ranks Tuple rather than List.
External source types must map into the entity model; unsupported SQL column types must be blacklisted or coerced in a custom query, and mappings differ across database drivers.
SQL Server's documented numeric mappings are INT/TINYINT to Integer, BIGINT/NUMERIC/DECIMAL to Decimal, FLOAT/REAL to Float, and BIT to Boolean with 0 false and 1 true.

SQL Server maps CHAR/VARCHAR/NVARCHAR/XML to String and UNIQUEIDENTIFIER to UUID; DATE/DATETIME map to Datetime with timezone-bearing values shifted to UTC, while DATETIME2 and TIME are driver-formatted strings and datetime-parse can convert DATETIME2.

Oracle's documented mappings are INTEGER to Integer, NUMBER to Float depending on column definition, BINARY_FLOAT/BINARY_DOUBLE to Float, CHAR/VARCHAR/VARCHAR2/CLOB/NCLOB/XMLType to String, BLOB/RAW/LONG RAW to Bytes, and DATE/TIMESTAMP to Datetime with timezone-bearing values shifted to UTC.

MySQL maps INT/TINYINT/BIGINT/BIT/BOOLEAN/YEAR to Integer, with BIT/BOOLEAN represented as 0 or 1 and YEAR documented as 1901–2155; NUMERIC/REAL/DOUBLE/DECIMAL map to Decimal while FLOAT maps to Float.

MySQL maps CHAR/VARCHAR/TEXT/TINYTEXT/TIME to String; BINARY/VARBINARY and TINYBLOB/MEDIUMBLOB/BLOB/LONGBLOB to Bytes; DATETIME/DATE/TIMESTAMP to Datetime; ENUM/SET vary with their underlying types and SET is a list.
MySQL DATE becomes a Datetime at midnight, its DATETIME import shifts timezone-bearing values to UTC, and its TIME strings use hh:mm:ss[.nnnnnnn].

PostgreSQL maps INTEGER/SMALLINT/BIGINT to Integer, NUMERIC/DECIMAL to Decimal, REAL/DOUBLE to Float, BOOLEAN to Boolean, CHAR/VARCHAR/TEXT/DATE/TIME/UUID/XML to String, TIMESTAMP to Datetime, BYTEA to Bytes, and ENUM according to enum type.

PostgreSQL DATE is a YYYY-MM-DD String and TIME a driver-formatted hh:mm:ss[.nnnnnnn][+|-tz:offset] String; timezone-bearing TIMESTAMP values shift to UTC, and PostgreSQL UUID is String unlike SQL Server UNIQUEIDENTIFIER's UUID mapping.

The SQL mapping reference contains legacy tested-version statements and describes several native temporal ranges as unlimited to nanosecond precision, whereas the entity Transit wire-type reference gives bounded Date and Datetime ranges.

Namespaces preserve attribute origin for multi-source merging and late schema binding; an attribute x first created in pipe y normally becomes y:x, while namespace-aware copying preserves existing property namespaces.

The overview concepts.rst sentence saying attribute x in pipe y becomes x:y contradicts its own examples and the focused namespace feature and DTL references, which establish namespace-first y:x placement.

A namespaced _id retains the reserved property name and stores a string value; property names and colon-bearing strings are distinct from typed NI and URI values, and colon syntax alone does not make a string an NI or URI.
namespaced_identifiers defaults false in service metadata and is inherited by pipes unless overridden; pipe namespaces.identity and namespaces.property independently default to the pipe id.

add_namespaces adds current identity namespace to _id and property namespace to properties before the first transform, normally inbound; remove_namespaces removes namespaces from _id, properties, and NI values after the last transform, normally outbound.

When namespaced_identifiers is enabled in service metadata, documented add_namespaces source defaults are true for csv, kafka, ldap, sql, embedded, http_endpoint, and json; documented remove_namespaces sink defaults are true for csv_endpoint, elasticsearch, mail, rest, sms, solr, kafka, sql, http_endpoint, and json.

Service metadata is the special configuration entity with _id node and type metadata, editable through configuration, UI, or Service API; namespaces.default is a namespace-to-URI expansion dictionary used by RDF-capable components rather than a pipe identity/property namespace selector.
Built-in URI expansion mappings are available unless explicitly overridden for _, rdf, rdfs, owl, foaf, wgs84, xsd, dc, skos, dcterms, and gs; _ maps to http://example.org/.
global_defaults.symmetric_namespace_collapse defaults false; enabling it changes RDF/SPARQL URI/NI collapse and expansion so that inbound and outbound mappings are symmetrical.
ni-collapse and ni-expand DTL functions are deprecated despite still being mentioned in service metadata documentation.

add, add-if, default, make-ni, remove, copy, rename, and path are namespace-aware; unqualified property references generally match across namespaces and wildcard patterns respect the boundary, with copy/remove patterns using the last colon as separator.

Namespace-aware add prefixes unqualified properties with the current property namespace and _id string values with the identity namespace, while preserving fully qualified properties; copy can match across namespaces, and rename preserves namespaces for an unqualified target or collects values into a fully qualified target.

In DTL namespace-aware argument syntax, :: means interpret the following value as-is and : means relative to the current identity or property namespace according to context; these escapes are separate from Transit encoding.

ni constructs typed NIs without string escaping, uses the global namespace when NAMESPACE is omitted, and accepts URI values only without that argument, collapsing prefixes to declared or generated namespaces.
uri casts string input values to typed URIs without URI escaping; explicit URL quoting is a separate operation.
The RDF source maps subject URIs to _id, predicate URIs to property names, and literals or URI objects to values, turning RDF blank nodes into child entities.

RDF output represents nested entities as blank nodes, lists as repeated predicates, and property types as RDF datatypes; language tags are unsupported and receivers lacking blank-node support require flattened output.

The documented local configuration-test workflow uses sesam -vv test, an expected directory, and paired endpoint output .json and .test.json files; test configuration can select stages or publisher endpoints and blacklist properties.
The documented local-testing output removes internal properties other than _id and _deleted, so fixture comparison alone does not verify _hash, _ts, _updated, or _previous metadata.
